classification.difficultyReason: Using the fixed-vertex hint, the student must translate an obtuse angle into a restriction on two circular positions, calculate its probability, and combine three mutually exclusive obtuse-angle events.

content.prompt:
Three points $A,B,C$ are chosen uniformly on the boundary of a circle. Find the probability that $\triangle ABC$ is acute.

Hint: Fix point $B$. Recall that the angle at $B$ is $90^\circ$ if and only if the other two points $A$ and $C$ are endpoints of a diameter.

answer.short:
$\frac14$.

For each vertex, the probability of an obtuse angle is $\frac14$. These events are mutually exclusive, so subtract their total probability from $1$.
answer.worked:
Fix $B$ and measure positions around the circumference from $B$ as fractions of one complete turn. Let the positions of $A$ and $C$ be $x$ and $y$. The pair $(x,y)$ is uniform in the unit square.

The arc between $A$ and $C$ that excludes $B$ occupies a fraction $|x-y|$ of the circumference. By the inscribed-angle theorem,
$$\angle ABC=180^\circ|x-y|.$$
Thus the angle at $B$ is obtuse when $|x-y|>\frac12$. In the unit square, this region consists of two corner triangles, each with perpendicular sides of length $\frac12$.
$$\begin{align*}
\Pr(B\text{ is obtuse})&=2\left(\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac12\right)\\
\Pr(B\text{ is obtuse})&=\frac14.
\end{align*}$$
The same probability applies at $A$ and $C$. A triangle cannot have two obtuse angles, and the probability of an exactly right angle is zero. Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
\Pr(\triangle ABC\text{ is acute})&=1-3\times\frac14\\
\Pr(\triangle ABC\text{ is acute})&=\frac14.
\end{align*}$$
